after: ## What does an introduction have to do?
alt: A doorway frames “the argument” inside, with an arrow for the reader walking in. Three labels point at the door: orient (introduce the subject and conversation), engage (give a reason to keep reading) and focus (point toward the claim).
caption: Orient, engage, focus: a doorway, not a room of its own.

after: ## The strategies available to a writer
alt: Eight cards for opening strategies, each with what it does well and what can go wrong: thesis first, quotation, intriguing statement, anecdote, question, statistic or data, contextual information and scenario.
caption: No opening is correct in itself; its effect must suit the situation.

alt: One claim, schools should start later, opened three ways: for a school board, context and a statistic about bus routes; for parents, a scenario of a tired teenager at 6:30 a.m.; for science-minded readers, an intriguing statement about body clocks followed by the thesis.
caption: Choose the opening by what this audience needs before it can listen.

after: ## Weak and strong introductions side by side
alt: The weak introduction (“Since the beginning of time... In this essay I will discuss both sides”) beside the strong one (a bus driver at 6:40 on a January morning, body clocks, and a clear claim). A scorecard compares how each orients, engages, focuses and wastes words.
caption: The strong version orients with a scene, engages with a reframing and ends on a claim.

after: ## Worked example 2: describing what a published introduction does
alt: Anthony’s opening sentence divided into parts: “I stand before you tonight under indictment” orients; “the alleged crime of having voted” engages, with “alleged” signalling a contest; “without having a lawful right to vote” focuses on the question the speech will answer. Her thesis that she “simply exercised” her rights follows later.
caption: Name the strategy, then its effect: orienting, engaging or focusing.
